utterances.text: Well, let me tell you I'm sure that there was a reason. If they burnt their houses, then they would have ascribed this to the Serbs, perhaps. That might be one of the reasons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if they looted their own property? Can you think of a good reason for looting one's own property and destroying one's own businesses?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO GVOZDENOVIC
utterances.text: No. I said that most probably -- I can't actually say for sure, tell you about something I didn't see. On our side I'm sure that there were people who abused that kind of thing and looted a Siptar house, but I'm talking about my own street where my neighbours, the Siptars, would give people their keys to look after their property, their homes. Isn't that proof enough that they had trust and confidence in our people?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you see, we've had some other proof in this case. There was a report that was submitted in this case that was called "Under Orders." This is Exhibit 145. It's a document produced by an organisation called Human Rights Watch. And it said that -- and I'm reading from page 290 of this report, where it was said that, "Within the first week of the war, an estimated 90 per cent of Pec's ethnic Albanian population had been forcibly expelled." You didn't see any of this activity where you were?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO GVOZDENOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. Can you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was quite clear. The same report on the same page said: "The ethnic cleansing operation in Pec was among the best organised in Kosovo, with buses waiting in the city centre to take people south towards Albania." Are you saying you didn't see any of this activity? Is that your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO GVOZDENOVIC
utterances.text: I -- if you listened to what I was saying carefully, then I said that this was going on in front of the post office and in the centre, and so that day or the following day I didn't see a single bus nor truck parked. And I've been telling you very clearly our police, our people, whenever they could, did their best to influence the Siptars, their compatriots, to prevail upon them not to leave because the Serbs know full well what population exoduses mean. They had many displacements themselves and know full well what that means and entails.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that this was going on in front of the post office. What was going on in front of the post office and in the centre? What was going on?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO GVOZDENOVIC
utterances.text: People had gathered there. They didn't know where to go. They were being -- the Siptars were forcing them out of their houses. Now, who would leave their homes just like that, without any reason? They had to do so under duress. They were coerced to do so. My house was set fire to, but I went -- if my house was set fire to, I would go back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's your testimony that there was a group of Albanians who were forcing other Albanians to leave their homes and go to Albania; right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO GVOZDENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely that. That's precisely what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO GVOZDENOVIC
utterances.text: There were decent, honest Siptars there who wanted to carry on living there together with us but we know the politics where it was created. You know that better than me, I'm quite sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Speaking of politics, let's just try to step back for a minute, and if you were an Albanian organisation trying to force people to leave their homes for political purposes, for purposes of political power, do you think it would be in your political interests to burn down those homes and their businesses behind them?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO GVOZDENOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, even if I was an Albanian, I would never advise that to anybody or tell them to do that. That's completely beyond all reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's assume that what you're saying is correct, that Albanians forced Albanians to leave their homes and go to the border. Can you think of any logical reason why the Albanian population at the border would feel compelled to leave all of their identity documents behind?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO GVOZDENOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't there, so I can't talk about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know a man named Ndrec Konaj in Pec?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO GVOZDENOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to ask the usher's assistance, please. If we could have a copy of Exhibit 3, map 6 placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a map produced by the Office of the Prosecutor showing routes that Kosovo Albanian citizens took when they left the city of Pec. You can see there is a green line heading to the north and then to the north-west into Montenegro, and we also see a green line heading south to the town of Prizren and then to the west again to the Albanian border. Do you see those lines?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO GVOZDENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ndrec Konaj testified to this Chamber -- and, Your Honour, I'm referring to Exhibit 112, and trial transcript 3778 to 3781 from the 25th of April, 2002. Mr. Konaj explained how he and his family were forced to leave their homes by Serbian police in the town of Pec, that homes were being set on fire by Serb forces, and that -- that they were placed on buses in the centre of Pec and then taken to the town of Prizren or close to the town of Prizren and subsequently put on other buses to the Albanian border, and that the Serb police in Pec not only organised this bus transportation but even provided the drivers of the buses. Are you saying you didn't see any of this activity?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO GVOZDENOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how it turns out now that the person that told you that and when I told you what I saw, that you believe him to be right. That's how it would appear, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a man named --

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO GVOZDENOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have proof of those buses? Were they filmed deporting those people, the trucks or whatever? Do you have any proof and evidence to show us?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a man named Besnik Sokoli?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO GVOZDENOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know him but I've heard of him. I've heard of the name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Besnik Sokoli testified in this courtroom on the 27th of February, 2002 - and this is at pages 1144 to 1155 of the transcript - and he describes how Serb forces were looting and burning homes in his neighbourhood in Pec, forcing residents to flee, how he began to walk with his family from Pec to the Montenegrin border, but then he was stopped by Serb police and told to go back to Pec because buses had been arranged to carry the Albanian population to Albania, and he subsequently walked back to the centre of Pec where there were thousands of Albanian citizens gathered, and during the course of the 27th and 28th of March, 1999, these thousands of people were placed on buses and driven to the Albanian border via Prizren. Is this all new to you?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO GVOZDENOVIC
utterances.text: I state again, do you have a picture today in the twenty-first century of those buses, of those trucks, showing the people being deported? Am I telling lies or am I telling the truth? All you're doing is showing me a map and making me look at the route they took. Everybody knows the route they took and what was going on and what happened and why they left. If you listen to me carefully, I explained that. They had two goals for leaving. One-- or two reasons: One, to show to the world their humanitarian catastrophe, and secondly, that the Serb people should be exposed to NATO bombing. That's the whole point of it, but I don't think you want to listen. You have your own -- well, things that suit you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after the end of March 1999, there were virtually no Albanians left in Pec; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO GVOZDENOVIC
utterances.text: Why don't you ask me whether after 1999, when KFOR entered, there was a single Serb left who had lived there for centuries? They had lived there for centuries. You keep asking me about the Siptars, whereas you know why I'm here and what you should be asking me about. You're asking me about the Siptars' deportation and I've told you why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Gvozdenovic, you must answer the questions to the best of your ability.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll repeat --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the questions are being repeated non-stop. If he asks a question, we can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If we find that they're repetitive, we'll say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question is after the end of March 1999, there were virtually no Albanians left in Pec; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO GVOZDENOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know from sources -- now, I wasn't able to bring in all the documents with me because I didn't know that's what we would be discussing and that you were going to ask me that. I would have brought you documents from the post office where I worked, where the Siptars on that day, before the Italians arrived, they suddenly appeared. Three thousand pension slips were handed out. Can you imagine? Three thousand people turned up to receive their pensions from the state of Serbia that they never recognised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO GVOZDENOVIC
utterances.text: So I don't know where they were until that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, would it be fair -- would it be fair to say that you feel some hostility towards the Albanian population of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO GVOZDENOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know how you came to that conclusion. I told you nicely that when I worked in the post office I had friends and sat with them and talked to them and tried to dissuade them from leaving their native town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll talk about how you --

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO GVOZDENOVIC
utterances.text: It's something that I wouldn't wish upon even my greatest enemy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll talk about that in a moment. Do you know a man called Edison Zatriqi?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO GVOZDENOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the surname is familiar but not the name, because there are many people with the surname Zatriqi in Pec.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Edison Zatriqi owned a bus company in Pec in 1998 and 1999. It was called Flamingo Tours. Does that ring any bells?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO GVOZDENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. He was a neighbour of mine, yes, from Flamingo Tours. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any -- any problems with Mr. Zatriqi's integrity?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO GVOZDENOVIC
utterances.text: He was a well respected citizen of Pec, as far as I know, and I think one of his sons worked in the state security service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Zatriqi testified in this court on the 25th of April, 2002 - and this is at page 3807 to 3808 of the transcript, and it's Exhibit 113 - and Mr. Zatriqi testified that on the 23rd of March 1999, the day before the NATO bombing campaign began, he was forced to turn over several of his buses to Serb policemen and that he subsequently saw his buses and buses being -- and buses owned by other Kosovo Albanian transport companies, he subsequently saw these buses being used to transport Kosovo Albanians to the border. Did you hear anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO GVOZDENOVIC
utterances.text: No. Truly I haven't heard about that, so I can't tell you about something I didn't see. All I'm telling you of is what I personally saw and where I personally was, and I stand by every word I say when I talk about things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, during your direct examination you talked about a lot of things that you didn't see, but I will move on. Mr. Zatriqi's buses were burned at the end of the war. Do you think that would be in Mr. Zatriqi's benefit to burn his property himself?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO GVOZDENOVIC
utterances.text: I tell you again, I didn't see it, and I can't talk about things that I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think it would have been in the -- to the benefit of the KLA or, as you call them, the bandits, to burn the property owned by Kosovo Albanians such as the buses owned by Mr. Zatriqi?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO GVOZDENOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see that, so I can't see whether they were bandits that set this on fire or what.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were a reserve police officer, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO GVOZDENOVIC
utterances.text: No. I worked in providing security for the post office and a private pizzeria, Pizza parlor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The truth is you know full well how the deportation of Kosovo Albanians from Pec occurred because you took part in it, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO GVOZDENOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. How do you mean "take part"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That you were a member of a paramilitary unit, and in particular you took part in the deportations of Catholic Albanians living on a street called Boro Vukmirovic in the town of Pec after the start of the NATO bombing campaign in March 1999, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO GVOZDENOVIC
utterances.text: No. How could I have been in a paramilitary unit if I worked as a security detail for the post office? There is documentation to bear that out. This is quite amazing. I don't know who supplied you with that kind of information. Can you show me the document showing a photograph of me deporting anyone, or is there a single Siptar here who testified ever mention my name and surname? Can you imagine? I'm a parent who came in here to talk about the violent killing of my child, and you ask me whether I deported somebody. Mr. President, this is really beyond all reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gvozdenovic, it's your testimony today, then, that you took absolutely no part -- remember you are testifying under oath today -- that you took absolutely no part in the deportation of Kosovo Albanian citizens in Pec? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO GVOZDENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. How could I have taken part in something when I worked as a security detail for the post office? You can find proof of that, that I provided security for buildings and facilities that were being safeguarded from being stormed by terrorists or bands of gangs. So we were providing security for socially-owned and state-owned property. And there are documents and lists to bear that out. I did shift work. You can see my shifts. This is quite ludicrous. I don't know where you get that from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as a person who worked in security matters, occasionally you had to travel around, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO GVOZDENOVIC
utterances.text: No. My house was quite near from my work, place of work, so I didn't need to use any transport.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the post office you worked at, that was in the centre of Pec, right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO GVOZDENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's your testimony today that you did not see any systematic deportation of Kosovo Albanian citizens from the centre of Pec in March of 1999? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO GVOZDENOVIC
utterances.text: I'm telling you again, while we were working, until I left work, when I come in the evening to take up my shift and duty, take over duty from the person before me, I would go round the facility, tour the facility. So when I toured the facility, I would meet my friends the Siptars when that happened. So let me repeat: I talked to them and I tried to dissuade them from leaving their homes. And let me tell you again, we Serbs know full well what it means to leave your homes. And I wouldn't even wish it upon my greatest enemy. So I keep repeating this same thing to you. I would like to see proof and evidence of my deporting anyone. Really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you try to dissuade from leaving their homes? Can you give us a name?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO GVOZDENOVIC
utterances.text: There were a lot of them, and I don't want to give the names of those people now because there can be repercussions. There can be repercussions. There are specific people in that respect. I don't want to put anybody into a difficult situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we please move into private session for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We will move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Are we in open session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified previously that you were never a member of the reserve police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO GVOZDENOVIC
utterances.text: During -- or, rather, 1979 I did my military service, and as a reservist, I was involved with the military but then there were more Siptars there then so they were the ones who were in command. I don't know why you're asking about this. Everybody knows this very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is very simple: Were you ever a member of the reserve police in Pec? Yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO GVOZDENOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. The reserve police, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Perhaps this could be distributed, marked for identification and given to the Judges. A copy can be given to the witness, please. Okay. If a copy could be placed on the ELMO, then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can take a look, sir, at the very first page. This is a document entitled "Formational posts of the reserve police department detachment (local community) Centar." Momir Radulovic is the commander, Stefan Stanjevic the deputy commander, and Dragan Vucinic assistant of the reserve police detachment. A little bit further down, it says Slobodan Zivkovic, the commander of the 2nd Company Puhovac, and then a little bit further down we see the first platoon at Patrijarsijska street. I'm sorry for my pronunciation, or lack thereof. On the next page we see the 2nd platoon at Pariska Street, and a bit further down we see two groups of names, and in the second group, at number 6, we see -- excuse me, at number 7, we see the name Zvonimir Gvozdenovic. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO GVOZDENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's you, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO GVOZDENOVIC
utterances.text: No. There's another Gvozdenovic in Pec. First of all, I do not live in Patrijarsijska Street. We have already established I live in Pariska, and there is major difference involved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This platoon is the platoon for Pariska Street. Is there another Zvonimir Gvozdenovic living, or who lived on Pariska Street?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO GVOZDENOVIC
utterances.text: No, but let me tell you I do not understand at all how my name got there, because I worked at the security for the post office, so I could not have been in this group at all. Everybody knows that very well. Would a state company allow me to go to some kind of paramilitary unit? And after all, these were not paramilitary units the way you want to portray them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, is the first name of this witness Zvonimir or Zvonko? Are they the same one?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It's my understanding that they are variations of the same name, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you clarify that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your formal name is Zvonimir, isn't it, sir, your formal first name?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO GVOZDENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I would ask that this be entered as an exhibit, Your Honour, if this is the appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be 867.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. And I believe we have some photographs, if the accused wishes to have them exhibited. We'll do that later. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one question, not to keep this witness any longer. I'm just going to put one question so he wouldn't have to stay during the break as well. Re-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gvozdenovic, you explained a few moments ago that you worked at the post office.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO GVOZDENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you said just now that towards the very end of the war, 3.000 Albanians came to receive their pensions at the post office.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO GVOZDENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that in response to what was said that the Albanians were driven out of Pec.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO GVOZDENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From who did they receive this pension at the post office?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO GVOZDENOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's well known; from the state of Serbia, not Albania.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So pensions are received once a month, right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO GVOZDENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on this same day, they all came and took their pensions?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO GVOZDENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Documentation is there and all of this can be established.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gvozdenovic.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO GVOZDENOVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Milosevic, do you want to have the photographs exhibited, and the video?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means. By all means. I tendered all of it. And also you can take the on-site investigation report and have it marked for identification, and also the other documents that you refused to admit because they had not been translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether we exhibited the previous witness's binder as D295, and we'll reserve the next number for the schedule, reference schedule, and then give this binder the next number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. So D296 will be reserved for the schedule, and then D297.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Have you given numbers for the video and the photographs?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 297, tab 1, tab 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. As we had indicated before, Mr. Milosevic, the untranslated reports will not be admitted. Mr. Gvozdenovic, that concludes your testimony. Thank you for coming to give it, and you may now leave. And we are adjourned for 20 minutes. We are adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, your next witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Radovan Paponjak is my next witness, Mr. Robinson, but now during the course of the break I established that he is not accessible. Professor Rakic informed me that last night an official from the Victims and Witnesses Unit in his presence said to Mr. Paponjak to be prepared at 2.15 to be transported to the prison in order to be able to see me. According to what Mr. Rakic knows, he went to church. He could not get in touch with him over the telephone, and he dialed both his mobile telephone number and his hotel. So he is not available, but through no fault of his own. As I said, last night the official concerned told him that he should be ready at 2.15 to be taken to see me at the prison. I am prepared to question him, but unfortunately, he is not here now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, is that the same witness as you thought had not been given clearance to give evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. That's Paponjak anyway, but he could probably have been dealt with by Mr. Milosevic for an hour until anything material to that issue was dealt with, then we've got the intervening week for the waiver to come through. So I think a decision had been taken just to get on with it and deal with him, which was my view anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So why -- well, you probably can't answer this, but why would Professor Rakic not make it clear that the arrangement was inappropriate?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The explanation don't make much sense to me at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No. Perhaps -- I think these are unrelated issues. I think they're not merged in any way. There was this other problem, but as a technical hitch on the waiver, the decision was made just to get on with it, which was in the interests of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, perhaps Mr. Milosevic can explain why Professor Rakic wouldn't make it clear that that was not an appropriate arrangement, that the witness would have to be here today.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot give an explanation. I only received this information from Professor Rakic, that your official from here told Mr. Paponjak to be ready today at 2.15 at the same time when he informed Jasovic and Gvozdenovic that they should be ready in the morning in order to be brought here. That is the only information I have, and I received just now during this last break. I did not ask Professor Rakic any additional questions because I didn't think that there was any need for me to put any other questions to him. May I just add that Professor Rakic tried to reach him by phone. In his hotel room there was no answer, and his cell phone is off. He tried to reach him from here. All in all, Mr. Paponjak is not absent through any fault of his own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, regrettably, we'll have to adjourn. We will lose -- we will have lost about an hour and 15 minutes. Mr. Milosevic, in future, I think all the -- all the arrangements must be made to ensure that your witnesses are present, within reason, of course. It's a little unclear to me why the witness is not here, notwithstanding the explanation that you have given. But we will adjourn, and we will resume on --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The 3rd of May is the new date, we believe. 4th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: On Wednesday, the 4th of May. We will resume on Wednesday, the 4th of May, at 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 4th day of May, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.50 p.m.,
